A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of batch-based temporal graph evaluation and fixed-horizon link forecasting. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original information-loss measurements and experiments comparing nine models across 14 temporal graph datasets, including sensitivity, runtime and information-leakage analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds empirical analyses of maximum information preservation and eligible negative-sampling pools.

M1.justification: The proposed fixed-duration forecasting windows, historical conditioning and window-level memory updates remain unchanged. Appendix G expands the previously described window-subdivision strategy into conceptual pseudocode; it does not establish a new model or a changed procedure in the reported experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight continuous-time and six discrete-time datasets, including the same realistic-horizon scenarios in Appendix E. Newly discussed routing, recommendation and traffic applications do not introduce evaluated datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain JODIE, DyRep, TGN, TGAT, CAWN, EdgeBank, TCL, GraphMixer and DyGFormer. The batch-size and snapshot-shuffling comparisons also retain their comparator membership. Additional related-work mentions do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v3 adds comparisons of maximum attainable NMI across batch-size/horizon choices and counts eligible historical and inductive negatives per batch/window. Existing training splits, budgets, evaluation metrics, batch sizes and forecasting horizons remain unchanged; the CPU fallback is newly disclosed implementation information.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a direct comparison of maximum information preservation, and Appendix A.2 investigates whether different negative-sampling pools could explain performance differences. These are targeted additions; the existing batch-size sensitivity, performance-over-time and snapshot-shuffling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 4 newly specifies that the five repetitions use different seeds. Both versions already report five runs and standard deviations, so this clarifies seed information without establishing additional runs or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Matched performance, runtime, sensitivity and shuffling tables retain their numerical values. New results include maximum NMI values, such as Canadian Parliament's 0.8316 for batching versus 1.0000 for windows in Table 2, negative-pool counts in Figure 8, and derived relative comparisons of existing realistic-horizon scores in Tables 8–9.

T1.justification: Definition 2.1 changes permitted history from strictly earlier timestamps to all edges in preceding batches, correcting an inconsistency with the discussed leakage mechanism. Section 2 also generalizes timestamps from natural to real numbers. Appendix B retains the NMI definition and worked derivation; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2's contribution statement suggests memory-based TGNNs are ill-suited for discrete-time data; v3 narrows this to batch-based evaluation overestimating their performance. The four diagnosed evaluation problems and fixed-horizon forecasting contribution remain, with added emphasis on applications such as opportunistic routing.

C2.justification: Appendix E.1 adds substantive guidance balancing task requirements, temporal irregularity and computational resources when choosing horizons. Section 5 expands the ranking-evaluation discussion to explain which problems it mitigates and how it can aggravate leakage, and develops hypotheses about window-based training and robustness. v2 mentioned these limitations but lacked these detailed applicability and mechanism arguments.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly discloses CPU fallback for GPU memory overflows and supplies basic and subdivided-window evaluation pseudocode, expanding v2's brief implementation discussion. v3 also adds dataset licensing information and a direct experiment-script link. Listed hardware and model hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds application literature on opportunistic routing, session-based recommendation and traffic forecasting, alongside Rossi et al. (2023) on temporal graph representations. These broaden motivation and horizon-selection context while retaining the existing positioning relative to UTG, TGNN training methods and evaluation benchmarks.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem explanations, results narrative and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Appendices A and E gain structured subsections, runtime material moves into a dedicated Appendix G, and the former detailed-results Appendix G becomes H. These changes substantially revise the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 1, adds an experimental-setup diagram, and presents the main performance comparisons as heatmaps and aggregate plots while retaining the original tables in Appendix H. It adds diagnostic figures, runtime plots and code listings, and replaces the main text's two-column format with a predominantly single-column layout.

improvement.justification: v3 improves clarity and practical usability through clearer diagrams, the corrected batch-history definition, a narrower memory-model claim, horizon-selection guidance and disclosure of CPU fallback. The added diagnostics provide incremental support: the negative-sampling check compares pool sizes rather than establishing equivalent sampled sets. The principal experimental evidence remains unchanged, making the overall gain useful but bounded.
